Ilex | species = ilex | authority = [[Carl Linnaeus|L.]] | status = LC | status_system = IUCN3.1 | status_ref = {{cite iucn |author=Rankou, H. |author2=M'Sou, S. |author3=Barstow, M. |author4=Harvey-Brown, Y. |author5=Martin, G. |date=2017 |title=''Quercus ilex'' |volume=2017 |article-number=e.T62537A3116134 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2017-3.RLTS.T62537A3116134.en |access-date=19 November 2021}} | range_map = Quercus_ilex range.svg | range_map_caption = Species' distribution: ''Q. ilex'' (green), ''[[Quercus rotundifolia|Q. rotundifolia]]'' (rose) }} The '''holm oak''' (''Quercus ilex''), also called the '''holly oak''',{{cite book | last=Mitchell | first=Alan F. | title=A Field Guide to the Trees of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher=Collins | publication-place=London | date=1974 | isbn=0-00-212035-6 | page=237}}{{cite book | last=Rushforth | first=Keith | title=Trees of Britain and Europe | publisher=Trafalgar Square Publishing | publication-place=London | date=1999 | isbn=0-00-220013-9 | page=1069}} is a large [[evergreen oak]] native to the [[Mediterranean region]]. It is a member of the [[section (botany)|section]] ''[[List of Quercus species#Section Ilex|Ilex]]'' of the genus,{{cite journal|doi=10.1006/mpev.1999.0614 |title=Phylogeny, Biogeography, and Processes of Molecular Differentiation in Quercus Subgenus Quercus (Fagaceae) |year=1999 |last1=Manos |first1=Paul S. |last2=Doyle |first2=Jeff J. |last3=Nixon |first3=Kevin C. |journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=333–349 |pmid=10413627|bibcode=1999MolPE..12..333M |s2cid=17068984|url=https://ericlwalters.com/Manos_etal_1999.pdf }}{{Citation |last1=Denk |first1=Thomas |chapter=An Updated Infrageneric Classification of the Oaks: Review of Previous Taxonomic Schemes and Synthesis of Evolutionary Patterns |date=2017 |title=Oaks Physiological Ecology. Exploring the Functional Diversity of Genus Quercus L. |pages=13–38 |editor-last=Gil-Pelegrín |editor-first=Eustaquio |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-69099-5_2 |isbn=978-3-319-69099-5 |last2=Grimm |first2=Guido W. |last3=Manos |first3=Paul S. |last4=Deng |first4=Min |last5=Hipp |first5=Andrew L. |editor2-last=Peguero-Pina |editor2-first=José Javier |editor3-last=Sancho-Knapik |editor3-first=Domingo}} with [[acorn]]s that mature in a single summer. ==Description== It is a large [[evergreen]] tree, attaining in favourable places a height of {{Convert|21–28|m|abbr=off}}, and developing in open situations a huge head of densely leafy branches as much across, the terminal portions of the branches often pendulous in old trees. The tallest recorded, a tree planted at [[Windsor Great Park]], is 30.4 m tall.{{cite web | title=The thickest, tallest, and oldest Holm Oaks (Quercus ilex) | website=Monumental trees | url=https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/trees/quercusilex/records/ | access-date=2024-11-11}} The trunk is sometimes over {{Convert|6|m|abbr=on}} in girth. The young shoots are clothed with a close grey felt. The [[leaves]] are very variable in shape, most frequently [[leaf shape|narrowly oval or ovate-lanceolate]], {{Convert|4–8|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} long (rarely to 10 cm long), 2–5 cm wide (rarely to 8 cm wide), rounded or broadly tapered at the base, pointed, the margins usually [[Glossary of botanical terms#entire|entire]] on mature trees, or (especially on young trees) more or less spiny-toothed. When quite young, both surfaces are clothed with whitish down, which soon falls away entirely from the upper surface, leaving it a dark glossy green; on the lower surface it turns grey or tawny, and persists until the fall of the leaf; the [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] is {{Convert|3–16|mm|frac=8}} long. The [[acorn]]s are produced one to three together on a short downy stalk, ripening the first season; they are usually 12–20 mm long in the UK, the cups with adpressed, downy scales, and an often wavy margin.Bean, W. J. (1976) ''Trees and shrubs hardy in the British Isles'' 8th ed., revised. John Murray. File:Ghjandi.jpg|Mature acorns on a tree in [[Corsica]] File:Quercus ilex0.jpg|Leaves and catkins in spring File:Quercus ilex MHNT.2006.0.1268.JPG|''Quercus ilex'', [[MHNT]] ==Distribution and habitat== Holm oak grows in pure stands or mixed forest in the Mediterranean and often at low or moderate elevations, but also at higher altitudes in the [[Atlas Mountains]]. It is native from westernmost [[Turkey]] and through [[Greece]] west to parts of the [[Iberian Peninsula]], where it mixes with ''Q. rotundifolia'', along the northern Mediterranean coastal belt, and in the Atlas Mountains in [[Tunisia]] and [[Algeria]]. ==Taxonomy== ''Quercus ilex'' is placed in [[Quercus sect. Ilex|section ''Ilex'']].{{Cite journal |last1=Denk |first1=Thomas |last2=Grimm |first2=Guido W. |last3=Manos |first3=Paul S. |last4=Deng |first4=Min |last5=Hipp |first5=Andrew L. |date=2017 |title=Appendix 2.1: An updated infrageneric classification of the oaks |website=figshare |doi=10.6084/m9.figshare.5547622.v1 |url=https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Appendix_2_1_________An_updated_infrageneric_classification_of_the_oaks/5547622/1 |access-date=2023-02-18 |format=xls |name-list-style=amp }} The closely related species ''[[Quercus rotundifolia]]'' was previously thought to be a [[subspecies]] of ''Q. ilex'', but is now more often treated as a separate species.{{cite web | title=Plants of the World Online | website=Plants of the World Online | date=2020-10-13 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:296290-1 | access-date=2024-11-11}} Some authors still describe ''Quercus rotundifolia'' as a subspecies of ''Quercus ilex''.{{cite web | last1=Rigo | first1=Daniele de | last2=Caudullo | first2=Giovanni | title=Quercus ilex in Europe: distribution, habitat, usage and threats | website=ResearchGate | date=2016-03-21 | url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/299471337 | access-date=2024-11-11}}{{cite web |title=''Quercus rotundifolia'' Lam. (1785) |url=http://www.oaknames.org/search/fullname.asp?id=592 |publisher=International Oak Society |access-date=31 December 2020 |archive-date=8 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408030117/http://www.oaknames.org/search/fullname.asp?id=592 |url-status=dead }} ==Etymology== The resemblance of the foliage to that of the common [[European holly]], ''Ilex aquifolium'', has led to its common and botanic names. The species name ''{{lang|la|ilex}}'' was originally the classical [[Latin language|Latin]] name for the holm oak, but later adopted as a botanical genus name for the hollies. The common name 'holm oak' takes its name from ''[[wikt:holm|holm]]'', an ancient name for holly.{{cite web |title=holm etymology |url=https://etymologeek.com/eng/holm/35173186 |access-date=30 December 2021 |website=Etymologogeek}} ==Cultivation and uses== The [[wood]] is hard and tough, and has been used since ancient times for general construction purposes as pillars, tools, wagons (as mentioned in [[Hesiod]], ''[[Works and Days]]'' on page 429), vessels and wine casks.{{cite web |title=Holm Oak {{!}} The Wood Database - Lumber Identification (Hardwood) |url=https://www.wood-database.com/holm-oak/ |access-date=13 March 2021}} It is also used as firewood and in [[charcoal]] manufacture.{{cite journal |last1=Uzquiano |first1=P. |last2=Ruiz-Zapata |first2=MaB. |last3=Gil-Garcia |first3=MaJ. |last4=Fernández |first4=S. |last5=Carrión |first5=J. S. |title=Late Quaternary developments of Mediterranean oaks in the Atlantic domain of the Iberian Peninsula: The case of the Cantabrian region (N Spain) |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016QSRv..153...63U/abstract |journal=Quaternary Science Reviews |access-date=13 March 2021 |pages=63–77 |doi=10.1016/j.quascirev.2016.10.013 |date=1 December 2016|volume=153 |bibcode=2016QSRv..153...63U }} The holm oak is one of the top three trees used in the establishment of [[truffle]] orchards, or [[truffière]]s. Truffles grow in an [[ectomycorrhizal]] association with the tree's roots.{{cite web |title=The Natural Gardener |url=https://thenaturalgardener.co.uk/truffle_trees.php |website=thenaturalgardener.co.uk |access-date=13 March 2021}} The first trees to be grown from acorns in England are still to be found within the stately grounds of [[Mamhead Park]], [[Devon]]. From Britton & Brayley in ''[[The Beauties of England and Wales]]'' (1803):
The woods and plantations of Mamhead are numerous and extensive. Many of them were introduced by Mr Thomas Balle (sic), the last of that family who, on returning from the continent, brought with him a quantity of cork, ilex, wainscot, oak; Spanish chestnut, acacia, and other species of exotic trees.Britton, J. & Brayley, E. W. (1803). ''Beauties of England & Wales''. Vol. 4: ''Devon & Cornwall'', Devonshire, p. 99. Various publishers.
Holm oak is not officially listed as an [[invasive species]] in the United Kingdom but is [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]], able to naturally regenerate. Normally the tree is unable to withstand severe frost, which would prevent it from spreading north, but with climate change, it has successfully penetrated and established itself in areas north of its native range.BBC News, 2008 The largest population of holm oak in Northern Europe is present on and around [[St. Boniface Down]] on the [[Isle of Wight]] and into the neighbouring town of [[Ventnor]], a town known for its naturally warmer [[Ventnor#Climate|microclimate]], and has shown to tolerate the high winds on the downs. It is thought that this population's propagation (which was established in the late 1800s after having been planted by Victorian residents) has been bolstered by native [[Eurasian jay]]s (''Garrulus glandarius''), which harvest acorns from oak trees and store them by burying them in the ground where they may then germinate. Feral goats were brought to Ventnor to control the spread of the holm oak.{{cite web|title=The holm oaks of Ventnor Downs|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ventnor-downs/features/the-holm-oaks-of-ventnor-downs|website=[[National Trust]]|access-date=9 May 2018}} It can be clipped to form a tall [[hedge (gardening)|hedge]], and it is suitable for coastal [[windbreak]]s, in any well drained [[soil]]. It forms a picturesque rounded head, with pendulous low-hanging branches. Its size and solid evergreen character gives it an imposing architectural presence that makes it valuable in many urban and garden settings. While holm oak can be grown in much of maritime northwestern Europe, it is not tolerant of cold continental winters.{{cite web |title=Buy Evergreen Oak Hedging Plants Online. Evergreen Oak for Sale Direct from Our Tree Nursery |url=https://www.kingco.co.uk/instant-hedging/evergreen-oak-quercus-ilex |website=www.kingco.co.uk |access-date=13 March 2021 |archive-date=22 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201022234603/https://kingco.co.uk/instant-hedging/evergreen-oak-quercus-ilex }} It is a parent of ''[[Quercus × turneri]]'', along with ''[[Quercus robur]]''. Holm oak was introduced to California in 1858 and is now a widely planted and locally naturalised species; it is often called "holly oak" there.{{Cite web |date=2010-01-17 |title=Tree of the Week: Holly oaks make good street trees |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/blogs/money-company/story/2010-01-17/tree-of-the-week-holly-oaks-make-good-street-trees |access-date=2023-10-24 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=SBB |date=2020-10-01 |title=Holly Oak |url=https://sbbeautiful.org/holly-oak/ |access-date=2023-10-24 |website=Santa Barbara Beautiful |language=en-US}} ==Notable trees== [[The Tree Register]] Champion in Gloucestershire measured 8.95 m in circumference and 12 m in height in 1993. Another tree at Courtown House, [[Wexford]], Ireland, reputedly planted in 1648, measured 20 m in height, with a spread of 43 m in 2010.Johnson, O. (2011). ''Champion Trees, of Britain & Ireland'', Kew Publishing, London. {{ISBN|9781842464526}} An ancient tree reputed to be 500 years old at [[Fulham Palace]], London is listed as one of the [[Great Trees of London]].Editors of Time Out (2010). ''The Great Trees of London'', Time Out, London. {{ISBN|9781846701542}} The oldest holm oak in Spain, the Encina Tres Patas de [[Mendaza]], located in [[Navarre]], is reputed to be 1,200 years old. A specimen in [[Milo, Italy|Milo]], in [[Sicily]], is reputed to be 700 years oldSee [http://www.comunedimilo.ct.it/illecciosecolare.htm the article about the tree] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417031837/http://www.comunedimilo.ct.it/illecciosecolare.htm |date=2020-04-17 }} while a small population on the slopes of northern village of Wardija in [[Malta]] are said to be between 500 and 1,000 years old. Prior to the Carthaginian period, holm oak was prevalent on the islands.Flora of the Maltese Islands, Hans Christian Weber, Bernd Kendzior, 2006, Margraf Publishers p. 184 {{ISBN|9783823614784}} Several holm oaks sit atop the 45 metre (148 ft) tall, 14th century [[Guinigi Tower]] in [[Lucca]], Italy, making it a notable tourist attraction for the city. The Roman poet [[Horace]] predicted that the ilex growing on his farm would become famous when he included it in his hymn to the Spring of Bandusia there (Odes 3.13.12–16):
fies nobilium tu quoque fontium,
me dicente cavis impositam ilicem
saxis, unde loquaces
lymphae desiliunt tuae.
(You will become one of the famous springs, too,
Now that I am telling of the ilex planted over your stone
Hollows, where your babbling
Waters leap down.)
